claims.text: Creating a heterostructured microstructure, such as a bimodal grain-size distribution, can overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in conventional metals.
Progressive strain partitioning between fine- and coarse-grained regions enables simultaneous improvements in strength and ductility.
The initial conventional metals have mostly homogeneous microstructures with uniform grain sizes.
Severe plastic deformation followed by controlled heat treatment can induce a bimodal or graded microstructure.
The induced microstructure contains distinct ultrafine-grained and coarse-grained zones.
Fine grains enhance strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
Fine- and coarse-grained zones enable progressive strain partitioning under load.
The heterostructured material will have higher yield strength than the conventionally processed homogeneous material.
The heterostructured material will have greater ductility than the conventionally processed homogeneous material.
Materials processed without microstructural heterogeneity exhibit high strength at the cost of reduced ductility.
The proposed benefit is expected to be most pronounced under monotonic loading.
The benefits of heterostructuring may be less significant under cyclic loading.
The benefits of heterostructuring may be less significant in materials with very high stacking-fault energies.
The magnitude of strength and ductility improvements depends on processing parameters and material composition.
